text:
A suspension bridge is a masterful feat of engineering that transfers the immense weight of a roadway and its traffic into the earth through a carefully orchestrated chain of tension and compression. The journey begins at the deck itself. The deck, which carries the vehicles and pedestrians, is not simply hung from the cables; it is a rigid structural element in its own right. As a load crosses the span, the deck works to distribute that concentrated force along its length, spreading it out to prevent a single point from bearing the brunt. This longitudinal stiffness is crucial, as it allows the load to be shared by multiple vertical suspender cables rather than causing a local deformation of the roadway.

From the deck, the load transfers upward into the network of vertical suspenders, which are typically thin steel ropes or rods. These suspenders act as the immediate messengers of weight, pulling downward at their top ends as they are tugged by the deck below. Their tops are attached to the massive main cables, which sweep in a gentle, catenary curve between the bridge’s towers. It is here that the true genius of the structural system becomes apparent. The main cables are in pure tension. As the vertical suspenders pull down with the load, they stretch the main cables, causing them to flatten slightly and try to straighten out. This tension force is what creates the characteristic dip of the cable, and it acts along the entire length of the cable, pulling toward both sides of the bridge.

The main cables are anchored at either end. They pass over the tops of the two or more towers and then descend to massive anchorages—enormous blocks of concrete and steel buried deep in the ground or extending into solid bedrock. At those anchorages, the tremendous horizontal pull of the cables is resisted, and the tensile force is converted into compressive stress on the earth itself. Meanwhile, the towers play a pivotal role. Standing atop piers or caissons driven into the riverbed or ground, the towers are in pure compression. The downward pull of the main cable on the tower top, combined with the weight of the tower itself, creates massive compressive forces that travel straight down the tower's height and are then spread over a large area by the foundation, allowing the ground to support the load without sinking.

Essentially, the load path is a continuous circuit of forces. The live load on the deck pulls down on the suspenders, which pull down on the main cables. The main cables, being in tension, pull horizontally inward toward the anchorages and vertically downward onto the towers. The towers, being in compression, push down into the earth. The anchorages, being fixed, pull against the earth. In this way, the weight of the bridge and its traffic is never held up by a single point, but rather is gracefully distributed through a symphony of tensile forces in the cables and compressive forces in the towers, ultimately finding its rest in the solid ground beneath and the stubborn grip of the anchorages.
